Isocyanide-Induced Annulation Leading to Cyclopento ‑, Methano ‑,
and Cyclopentano-[60]Fullerene Derivatives
Yanbang Li, William P. Kopcha, Thomas J. Emge, Yue Sun, and Jianyuan Zhang *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 8867 −8872 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: The three-component annulation reactions of C 60,
alkyl isocyanide, and dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate (DMAD) or
unsymmetric alkynes are investigated to a ﬀord cyclopent-2-en-1-
imino- and ketenimine methano-[60]fullerene derivatives, which,
upon hydration in the presence of acid, yield the corresponding
fullerene amides. Dimethyl 2,3-pentadienedioate, the allene
counterpart of DMAD, and ethyl buta-2,3-dienoate undergo four-
component annulation with C
60, alkyl isocyanide, and water under
similar conditions to yield cyclopentano-[60]fullerene derivatives
with similar amide groups.
F
ullerenes are promising building blocks in biomedicine, 1
organic and perovskite solar cells, 2 (photo)electrocatalytic
systems, 3 and simple structural sca ﬀolds for functional
materials4 due to their physicochemical, electrochemical, and
photophysical properties and structural characteristics. Re-
gioselective functionalization reactions of fullerenes have been
actively sought after to improve the synthetic yield and the
structural diversity of fullerene derivatives to realize their
potential.
5
Multicomponent reactions involving alkyl isocyanide and sp-
hybridized carbon reactants (i.e., alkynes, 6 allenes7) have been
widely used to construct cyclic structures in organic synthesis.
These reactions are underexplored for the functionalization of
fullerenes. The sole example, which is among an alkyl
(cyclohexyl or t-butyl) isocyanide, a special alkyne dimethyl
acetylenedicarboxylate (DMAD), and C
60, was reported to give
two C 60 derivatives: [3 + 2] cycloadduct 1 and [2 + 2]
cycloadduct 2 (Scheme 1a).8 However, even in this report, the
structural elucidation of the derivatives left major questions.
Recently, we reported the multicomponent reaction of a
metallofullerene Lu
3N@Ih-C80, t-butyl isocyanide ( tBuNC),
and terminal or internal alkynes. 9 When DMAD was used as
the alkyne, metallofulleroid 3 (Scheme 1 a) with a ketenimine
group formed, which was unambiguously con ﬁrmed by a
single-crystal study. This result was very di ﬀerent from the
reported C 60 reactions. To fully understand the DMAD
reaction and, more importantly, the substrate scope of reaction
regarding other alkynes and allene reactants, we performed a
systematic study of multicomponent reactions among
tBuNC,
a series of sp carbon reagents, and C 60. We found that the
reaction of DMAD, C 60, and alkyl isocyanide would a ﬀord
traditional [3 + 2] products similar to 1 and [1 + 2] adducts
similar to 3,a sw a sc o n ﬁrmed by crystal data. Three-
component reactions involving unsymmetric alkyne substrates
that meet certain criteria could also give similar results.
Additionally, the four-component reactions of allene sub-
strates, dimethyl 2,3-pentadienedioate or ethyl buta-2,3-
dienoate, C
60, tBuNC, and water yielded cyclopentano-
[60]fullerene derivatives.
The reaction was ﬁrst carried out with C 60, tBuNC, and
DMAD in o-dichlorobenzene ( Scheme 1 b). Two products,
later identi ﬁed as the traditional [3 + 2] adduct 4a8 and
ketenimine methanofullerene 5a, respectively, were detected
within a few minutes. The yields of 4a and 5a were strongly
aﬀected by the stoichiometry and the reaction time, as too high
equivalents of the isocyanide and alkyne or a too long reaction
time would lead to high-polarity mixtures that are insoluble in
common solvents. Cyclohexyl isocyanide reacted in a similar
fashion, yielding 4b and 5b. In both cases, the products 5 (a
and b) were dominant. Furthermore, the hydrolysis of 5a and
5b under acidic conditions gave compounds 6a and 6b in high
yields, whereas 5b could gradually be converted to 6b in air.
All of the products were puri ﬁed by ﬂash chromatography,
and the spectroscopic data ( Figures S1 −S36)o f 4−6 agree
with the structures shown in Scheme 1b. Matrix-assisted laser-
desorption ionization time-of- ﬂight mass-spectrometry
(MALDI-TOF MS) con ﬁrmed the molecular weights of 4−

6. All 1H, 13C, and 1H−13C heteronuclear multiple quantum
coherence (HMQC) NMR spectra of 4a and 4b clearly
pointed toward the 1,3-dipolar addition product ( Cs
symmetry), consistent with the previous report. 8 However, in
theory, the position of the alkyl group can generate two
stereoisomers, with R being cis or trans to the fullerene cage,
which is an important aspect not addressed in the report.
8
Indeed, while we observed only one single isomer for 4a, the
13C NMR spectrum of 4b showed a set of minor peaks of ∼1/5
intensity due to the stereoisomerization. We hypothesized that
the observed stereoisomer of 4a and the major product in 4b
are the trans isomers because there is a large energetic cost for
the bulky t-butyl group to be cis to C
60 in the transition state,
whereas such cost is less prohibitive for a ﬂexible cyclohexyl
group. The structures of 5a and 5b were also elucidated based
on NMR. Taking 5a for example, the 13C NMR spectrum
(Figure S9 ) shows Cs symmetry with only one peak (74.5
ppm) for two sp 3 carbon atoms on the cage, which suggests
two functional groups being perpendicular to the reacted bond
on the cage, such as a bridgehead carbon atom in
methanofullerenes or fulleroids. On the basis of additional
1D and 2D NMR spectra ( Figures S11 −S13), the ketenimine
methanofullerene is the most likely product, similar to 3,
9
except that the C 60 derivative is a closed-cage methanofullerene
instead of an open-cage fulleroid based on the chemical shift of
two sp
3 carbon atoms on the cage (74.5 ppm for 5a, 74.2 ppm
for 5b). With the structures of 5a and 5b, the structures of
hydration products 6a and 6b can be easily derived with the
MS and 1D and 2D NMR characterizations.
To test our hypothesis on 4 and to con ﬁrm our structural
elucidation of 5, we performed single-crystal analysis on 4a and
5a (Figure 1, Figures S6 and S14 ). For 4a, the ﬁve-membered
ring at the [6,6] position was veri ﬁed with a clear trans
relationship between the fullerene cage and the t-butyl group,
as was predicted. The ketenimine methanofullerene structure
of 5a was also de ﬁnitively con ﬁrmed. On the basis of the high
similarity of 5a and 5b in almost every way (various 1D and
2D NMR spectra, polarity, etc.), we expect 5b to have the
same ketenimine group with a di ﬀerent substituent.
Given that our products 5 are di ﬀerent from the literature,
we repeated our reaction using
tBuNC in toluene, the same
solvent used in the original report, 8 to exclude the possibility of
the solvent e ﬀect resulting in di ﬀerent products. Still, the same
products 4a and 5a were obtained. A careful examination of
the 13C NMR spectrum revealed that our spectrum of 5a is
identical to the reported spectrum of 2, except with higher
signal-to-noise ( Figure S10 shows the comparison of the two
spectra). Although structure 2 was a plausible assignment at
the time, both spectra are more consistent with structure 5a.
More importantly, the structure of 5a was conﬁrmed by crystal
analysis, which was not performed in the previous report. 8
Therefore, we conclude that the same product was
misrepresented in the report 16 years ago given the sample
amount and experimental conditions back then. Correspond-
ingly, the correct hydration products were shown as 6 in the
scheme based on the structures of 5 and their NMR data.
To further understand the reaction, we then set out to
evaluate the scope of other alkyne reactants, as shown in
Scheme 2 . First, with one methyl ester group of DMAD
replaced, 7a
10 and 7c−f as well as additional terminal alkynes
7g, h were used as reactants and optimized with a range of
stoichiometry and reaction temperatures. Only 7a aﬀorded
similar products 8a and 9a, as in the DMAD reactions ( Figures
S37−S48), which indicates the importance of an electron-
withdrawing group (EWG) on a phenyl ring, such as the 4-
nitrophenyl group. During the process,
tBuNC attacked the α-
Co f 7a to generate the reactive 1,3- or 1,4-dipolar species, 9
which reacted with C 60 to yield 8a and 9a. The attacking
position, α-C, is proved by the 1H−13C heteronuclear multiple
bond coherence (HMBC) 2D NMR spectrum of 9a (Figure
S48), in which the aromatic protons interact with the newly
formed bridge carbon, whereas the methyl protons of the ester
group do not. In the next step, the hydration of 9a under the
same acidic conditions gave amide 10a (Figures S56−S61) and
another byproduct 11a (Figures S62 −S67) with a newly
formed cyano group.
The formation of these two compounds is due to the usual
transformation of the ketenimine group 11 in 9a. Encouraged by
the function of the 4-nitrophenyl group, we synthesized

compound 7j12 with two 4-nitrophenyl groups at both ends of
the CC triple bond, but it failed to give similar results, which
showed the key role of the ester group in stabilizing the α
carbanion intermediate. In addition, 7b13 with a C C double
bond conjugated with the C C triple bond, used in the
functionalization of C 60 mediated by PPh 3,13 was synthesized
and used in the tBuNC-induced reaction of C 60. Compound
9b, with the C C double bond remaining, was obtained as
the only isolable product ( Figures S49 −S55), which can be
converted into amide 10b (Figures S68 −S73) in the presence
of acid. The crystallization of these products was very
challenging, and after extensive optimization, we were only
able to get a decent crystal for 9b, which is shown in Scheme 2
and Figure S55. When the double bond in 7b was changed to a
triple bond, 7i
14 yielded a similar product in trace amount after
a much longer reaction time at a much higher temperature. In
summary, this reaction works when R
1 provides both an
electron-withdrawing inductive e ﬀect and a resonance e ﬀect
that stabilize the anionic intermediate.
The proposed mechanism for the formation of methano-
and cyclopropeno-fullerene derivatives is proposed in Scheme
3. Nucleophilic attacks of alkyl isocyanide on alkynes yield
zwitterionic species A and B.T h ec o n c e r t e d[ 3+2 ]
cycloaddition of B and C 60 generates typical [3 + 2] products
4 and 8a. Carbanion A reacts with C 60 to give fullerene anion
C, which could undergo two cyclization pathways: 5- exo-dig
and 3-exo-trig. The 5-exo-dig ring-closure of C also aﬀords [3 +
2] products 4 and 8a, whereas the 3- exo-trig ring closure forms
ketenimine derivatives 5 and 9. The ketenimine derivatives
have signi ﬁcantly higher yields than the [3 + 2] products,
indicating that the 3-exo-trig ring closure is favorable over the
5-exo-dig process in this case. The mechanism is similar to that
in our recent report on the Lu
3N@C80 reaction,9 except that
the [3 + 2] adduct is formed in an appreciable amount and the
rearrangement of methanofullerene forming open-cage fulle-
roids did not happen.
Another form of sp carbon atoms, cumulated alkenes, can
undergo cycloadditions with C
60 induced by phosphines. 15
Although a multicomponent reaction involving alkyl isocyanide
and allenoates has been widely used to construct cyclic
structures in organic synthesis,
7 such a reaction has never been
applied in the functionalization of fullerene to the best of our
knowledge. Replacing the triple bond with cumulated double
bonds, we performed the reaction of C
60, tBuNC, and the
allenoate counterpart of DMAD. Dimethyl 2,3-pentadiene-
dioate 12a
16 reacted with C60 and tBuNC and yielded only one
isolable product, later identi ﬁed as the 13a (Figures S74−S79),
with water involved in this process. Ethyl buta-2,3-dienoate
12b underwent a similar four-component annulation to form
13b (Figures S80 −S85).
MALDI-TOF spectra ( Figures S74 and S80 ) showed
molecular ion signals for 13a,b as the sum of all reactants
plus one molecule of water. The
1H, 13C, DEPT-135, and
HMQC NMR spectra ( Figures S75 −S79 and S81 −S85)o f
13a and 13b showed the formation of the 1,3-dipolar addition
products ( Cs symmetry). 1H and HMBC NMR spectra reveal
more detailed stereochemistry regarding the relative positions
of the amide and ester groups ( Scheme 4 ). For 13a, the
orientations of three special protons were determined as
follows: (1) The chemical shifts of H
a and Hc were signiﬁcantly
diﬀerent. (2) There were two di ﬀerent coupling constants
between H b and H a (3Jtrans ≈ 12.8 Hz) or H c (3Jcis = 6.8 Hz).
(3) In HMBC, H c interacts with C C, whereas H a and H b
interact with all three of the carbonyl carbons. Therefore, H a
and H c are nonequivalent; that is, they have di ﬀerent relative
positions with H b. The situation of 13b is further complicated
by the greater number of protons. The geminal coupling
between H
g and H h (2J ≈ 12.3 Hz) con ﬁrms the formation of

and H e (J ≈ 1.2 Hz) determines the cis orientations of these
two protons. The orientation of H d is based on the following
points: (1) There are three coupling constants between H d and
He (3Jcis = 6.6 Hz), H g (3Jtrans = 13.3 Hz), or H h (3Jcis = 6.2 Hz)
respectively. (2) In HMBC, among H e,H g, and H h, only H g
interacts with amide C D due to the cis orientations of H g and
CD.
On the basis of the literature 7,15 and our results, 9 we have
proposed the mechanism for the formation of 13, using 13a as
an example ( Scheme 5 ). tBuNC reacts with 12a to generate
intermediate D; then, the anionic carbon atom attacks the
[6,6] bond of C 60 to form the fullerene carbanion E, which can
undergo two cyclization pathways: 5- exo-dig and 5-endo-trig. In
this case, the favored 5- endo-trig ring closure of species E gives
species F with a ketenimine group. Similar to the hydration of
5 and 9 under acidic conditions, species F directly reacts with
water to a ﬀord compound 13a.
In summary, the three-component cycloaddition reaction of
C60, alkyl isocyanide, and DMAD is investigated to a ﬀord
cyclopent-2-en-1-imino- and ketenimine methano-[60]-
fullerene derivatives, as con ﬁrmed by single-crystal analysis.
Hydration of the ketenimine methanofullerene in the presence
of acid gives the corresponding fullerene amides. Additional
versions of alkynes have been tested as reactants under similar
conditions, which suggests that the reaction requires an ester
group on one side and a substituent providing both inductive
and resonance e ﬀects on the other side of the triple bond.
Furthermore, the four-component reaction of C
60,a l k y l
isocyanide, allenoates, and water is also investigated and
provides cyclopentano-[60]fullerene derivatives. The multi-
component annulation reaction involving allenoates will be
explored with other carbon cages, such as C
70 and endohedral
fullerenes.
